# AWS Lightsail Cost Saver

> Free calculator for Amazon Lightsail data transfer. Lightsail instances of the same size in the same AWS Region share one transfer allowance pool. Given a setup and this month's usage (or a month-end forecast), it says whether the month is safe, how much overage to expect, and the cheapest number of extra same-size IPv6-only "traffic instances" to add. Everything runs client-side; there is no server API.

- Web app: https://ls.1ms.dog/
- Source: https://github.com/yt1988/lightsail-cost-saver
- Prices (JSON): https://ls.1ms.dog/prices.json
- Calculation module (ES module): https://ls.1ms.dog/calc.js

## Billing rules the calculator applies

- Inbound and outbound traffic both count against the allowance; only outbound traffic beyond it is charged (overage, USD per GB, varies by region).
- Allowances pool across instances in the same region with the same bundle size; dual-stack and IPv6-only instances of one size pool together.
- 1 TB = 1024 GB. The billing month is the UTC calendar month. Mumbai, Sydney, Jakarta, Malaysia, Hong Kong and São Paulo get half the allowance (already reflected in prices.json).
- Instances are billed hourly; allowance for an instance that exists only part of the month is prorated by its lifetime.
- Overage already incurred cannot be offset by adding instances later; new instances only cover traffic from when they start.
- The base instance can be dual-stack or IPv6-only; traffic instances are always the base's size and IPv6-only (cheapest per TB).
- Results are estimates; the AWS bill is final. Not an official AWS tool.

## Option 1: send the user a pre-filled link

Build a URL and give it to the user. Opening it loads the setup into their browser (their previous data is backed up and can be restored).

```
https://ls.1ms.dog/?region=us-east-1&size=1&used=3150&nodes=1@2026-10-11T00:00Z
```

| Param | Meaning | Example |
|---|---|---|
| `region` | AWS Region code | `us-east-1` |
| `size` | base bundle, identified by RAM in GB: 0.5, 1, 2, 4, 8, 16, 32, 64 | `1` |
| `ipv4` | `0` = base is IPv6-only (default dual-stack) | `0` |
| `base` | base instance start (UTC ISO), default start of month | `2026-10-01T00:00Z` |
| `used` | data used so far this month in GB (in + out) | `3150` |
| `in`, `out` | used GB split by bill item (TotalDataXfer-In-Bytes / -Out-Bytes); summed | `150`, `3000` |
| `at` | when `used` was read (UTC ISO), default now | `2026-10-26T06:00Z` |
| `forecast` | expected month-end total GB; with no `used` this switches to full-month planning | `10000` |
| `outpct` | share of traffic that is outbound, 0–100 (default 100) | `90` |
| `prorate` | `0` = don't prorate mid-month allowance | `0` |
| `nodes` | traffic instances, comma-separated `count@start[~end]` (UTC ISO) | `2@2026-10-20T00:00Z,1@2026-10-25T00:00Z~2026-10-28T00:00Z` |

Users usually name a bundle by its price and transfer, as the web app shows it (for example "$7 / 2 TB"). Map that to `size` with prices.json: find the bundle in that region whose `dualStackMonthly` (or `ipv6OnlyMonthly` for an IPv6-only base) and `transferTB` match, and use its `ramGB`. Transfer is halved in some regions, so match within the user's region.

Add `lang=` (en, zh-CN, zh-TW, ja, ko, es, fr, de, pt, ru) to choose the interface language.

## Option 2: compute the answer yourself

In a browser, Deno, or any runtime that can import ES modules from a URL:

```js
import { calculate, buildLink } from "https://ls.1ms.dog/calc.js";
const prices = await (await fetch("https://ls.1ms.dog/prices.json")).json();

const input = {
  region: "us-east-1",
  sizeGB: 1,                // base bundle RAM
  ipv4: true,               // base is dual-stack
  usedGB: 3150,             // or inGB + outGB, or only forecastGB for a full-month plan
  trafficInstances: [{ count: 1, start: "2026-10-11T00:00Z" }]
};
const result = calculate(input, prices);   // optional 3rd arg: "now" in ms
const link = buildLink(input);             // the same setup as an Option 1 link
```

`calculate` returns plain JSON, the same numbers the web app shows:

```json
{
  "mode": "actual-usage",
  "status": "overage-expected",
  "allowanceGB": 3435.35, "usedGB": 3150, "forecastGB": 3867.33,
  "overageGB": 431.97, "overageCost": 38.88, "instanceCost": 10.38, "totalCost": 49.26,
  "allowanceRunsOutAt": "2026-10-28T…Z", "unavoidableOverageGB": 0,
  "recommendation": { "addTrafficInstances": 2, "startingAt": "2026-10-26T06:00:00.000Z",
    "eachAddsGB": 379.87, "eachCosts": 0.93, "resultingCost": 1.85, "savesVsAddingNone": 37.02 },
  "options": [{ "addTrafficInstances": 0, "instanceCost": 0, "overageCost": 38.88, "total": 38.88 }, "…"],
  "nextMonth": { "trafficInstances": 1, "monthlyCost": 12 }
}
```

- `mode`: `actual-usage` (usage given), `full-month-plan` (only a forecast; every instance counts for the whole month), `needs-input`.
- `status`: `safe`, `overage-expected`, `over-allowance` (overage already incurred), `needs-input`.
- Money is USD, transfer is GB, times are UTC ISO strings.

Node.js can't import from a URL directly: download calc.js next to your script, or copy the module from the repository (`public/calc.js`).

## prices.json

`regions[id].overagePerGB` and `regions[id].bundles[]` with `ramGB`, `dualStackMonthly`, `ipv6OnlyMonthly`, `transferTB`. `date` is when prices were last pulled from the AWS Price List API.
